utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. All the accused are here. Defence teams are all here except for Mr. Ostojic. The Prosecution, it's Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Nicholls, Mr. Thayer. All right. Is there anything wrong with Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, sir, Your Honour. He's working at the office this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we, over the weekend, and I'll come back to you because we discovered a couple of things that need to be addressed, due to obviously the rhythm at which we are working, sometimes this happens. Yes, I understand there are some preliminaries. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour. We just had a few exhibits. We didn't -- as you know, we all ran out of time with Dr. Haglund, but I have some exhibits just to offer into evidence at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Those are -- they're basically annexes of detailed information on his various reports that didn't make it on the 92 bis motion but were on the 94 bis motion, and they are P00612, 613, 614, 615, 617, 618, 619, 620, 623, 624, and 625. And that's -- should do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Any objections from any of the Defence teams? Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I, frankly, don't have that file with me today; but if you give me until the first break to talk to Mr. McCloskey, I'll see if I have any objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. So we'll decide on that later on. Any further preliminaries? Or not -- this was not a preliminary, it was a -- yes, a conclusion of the Haglund testimony. Yes, Ms. Condon.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. I have just a very brief oral submission to make to the Chamber. Your Honour, it concerns an item that appeared on the ICTY's intranet last week. I'm not sure if any of the members of the Trial Chamber read the item in question, but I'll indicate that it was -- appeared on the 14th of March, and it was headed, "ICTY spokesman denounces shameful denial of the Srebrenica genocide." As part of that item and at a press briefing given by an ICTY spokesman, Refik Hodzic, there was a comment made in this regard. He said that: "The ICTY wishes to condemn this as well as other recent attempts to deny the genocide committed in Srebrenica where more than 7.000 men and boys were killed. I strongly recommend that anyone wishing to debate about the events of Srebrenica would start by reading the judgements of this Court which establish facts after careful weighing of evidence produced by years of investigations, thousands of exhibits, testimonies of both survivors and perpetrators, all fully tested and confirmed by the International Court of Justice." Now, Your Honour, that may appear an innocuous comment at first glance because it's certainly one that has been made on a number of occasions in countless articles, books, media reports. The assertion has been made that genocide was committed in Srebrenica. There's no argument there. However, in -- on behalf of Mr. Popovic, the submission is that there is a significant -- there's two dangers in that comment in particular. Now, firstly, that is a comment that is coming from a spokesperson of the very institution where Mr. Popovic faces trial. That's the first point. And, secondly, accepting that you are professional judges and that your role is certainly not one where we can expect you would be swayed or influenced in any manner by such comments, I'm not making that submission, Your Honour. It's a slightly different submission. Because it doesn't impact upon the capacity of you as professional judges to ensure that Mr. Popovic receives a fair trial, it's at another level which is perception as to whether or not Mr. Popovic receives a fair trial. And in our submission that's equally as important as to whether or not he receives a fair trial, and that one may expect that if you were to suggest to somebody that a spokesperson from the very court where the person -- an accused is on trial has made comments which impact upon the manner in which an accused person has chosen to conduct their defence, then that may well undermine the perception of a fair trial. There is, in our submission, no doubt that when an accused person conducts their defence in the manner in which they see fit, they should not be exposed to comments such as this that -- that's condemned. Because Your Honours will know what the issues are between the Defence and the Prosecution in this trial, and certainly I don't need to go into that. But it has amounted to a denial, certainly, of the statement made by the ICTY spokesperson. And, as I said from the outset, Mr. President, Mr. Popovic feels aggrieved. I'm sure the Trial Chamber would appreciate that he is entitled to feel aggrieved by such statements being made by the spokesperson of this institution. And in that regard, I do draw your attention to the provisions of Rule 77, which deals with circumstances under which persons can be held to have knowingly and wilfully interfered with the administration of justice. Now, I simply draw the Court's attention to those comments and draw the Court's attention to the provisions of Rule 77, and I should also indicate to the Trial Chamber, we have, the -- the accused that are facing genocide in this trial have written a joint letter to the president of this Tribunal, and I say that because I don't want there to be any perception that there's any underhandedness by that -- by making that submission. But that was a slightly different redress that we sought there with this Tribunal's president. What we seek here is a consideration by this Trial Chamber as to whether or not he considers that there has been some inappropriate and improper interference with the perception of whether or not Mr. Popovic receives a fair trial in this Tribunal. They are the submissions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Condon. Do you wish to comment, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are free not to if you don't wish to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We just put up what she's referring to, and I believe it's something that was posted by the registry, Christian Chartier, and a person named Refik Hodzic. I'm sorry to say I don't know who that is, but it must be a registry person. We'll take a look at -- at the substance of it. The -- as far as I can tell, it's -- it's making reference to the previous genocide convictions, and the ICJ, which are known facts. I don't see anything particular to any of the accused here, which I think is important. But, having said that, we will take a look at it and see what we think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. I think I will consult with my colleagues in due course, and we'll come back to you on -- on this. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, for the record, the Defence for Mr. Ljubisa Beara also joins on the submission by the Popovic team. We believe it is completely inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I take it -- I don't think you all need to stand up one after the other. The way I read Ms. Condon's words was to the effect that this is something which -- on which you are four square. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I just wanted to say, because the charge of genocide does not concern my client, but due process does concern him. So in spite of the fact that this particular problem does not apply to my client, I fully join Ms. Condon on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. As I said, we'll come back to you. I trust, however, you do remember our previous decision on adjudicated facts, that was handed down after that in the case of the Rwanda Tribunal. It had been decided that there won't be any further discussions on whether genocide had taken place in Rwanda or not. In our case, the fact that genocide had or had not been committed in Srebrenica was not one of the adjudicated facts that we took. But in any case, we'll come back, because it's obviously a serious submission that you've made, Ms. Condon, supported by the rest, and we'll -- we will need to discuss it. But I don't think it should take more of our court time today. We'll certainly come back to you on it. All right. The other thing is this: That over the weekend, Friday and also yesterday, we were going through the pending matters related to the testimony of PW-101, and you will recall there is also a certification motion related to that witness. What happened was this: That -- I'm not going to address the documents that are subject to the certification motion, I'm going to address only three documents that were not objected to by Mr. Nicholls. Three documents that the Defence of Mr. Nikolic tried to -- or asked to be admitted, tendered into evidence, which Mr. Nicholls did not object to but which, due to an oversight, we failed to decide upon. I'm referring to documents number P295, Mr. Bourgon. P295, P311, and 1D217. You had tendered these, together with others. Mr. Nicholls objected to the admission of the two redacted statements, which you later withdrew, which you later withdrew. You decided not to tender them any further. But he had not objected to the tendering of these three documents that I mentioned. We got engulfed in the discussion on the other two documents and never decided to tender -- to accept, to admit the three documents that were not objected to. I suggest that you check on this, check that we are correct on this, both of you, please; and when after the break we decide on the documents to be tendered in relation to Professor Haglund, or Dr. Haglund, we will also decide on -- on these after the break. Okay? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. I was just wanting -- you mentioned something about that these documents were subject to certification. Is that not a different matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. These documents -- arising out of the testimony of PW-101, there are two issues pending; the certification, motion for certification that you filed, the Beara team and the Nikolic team.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That was 104, if I may, Mr. President. I believe this is 104 and not 101.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm talking of 101. Okay. So it's all right. But still we are talking of three documents that, as a result of the discussion that we had, remained undecided upon. So please have a look at those, and tell me whether we are correct or not. And we'll -- we'll decide later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: P295 was two pages of a vehicle work log; P311, log of troop presence; and 1D217, the certificate of, I think, the mother of the person who was supposed to be in charge of that place, that the witness spoke about. All right? And come back to us, please, after the break. Can we start with the next witness? Before we start, may I ask you to agree on the following: There are six witnesses that are due to testify one after the other in the course of this week and possibly early next week. These are witnesses number 156, 158, 124, 48, 168, and 16, who is an expert witness. These six witnesses were amongst the 12 that were included in the Prosecution submission, confidential submission to convert 12 viva voce witnesses to Rule 92 ter witnesses. These six witnesses are not amongst the ones that are being, or have been formally contested by the Defence teams. In other words, the Defence teams are challenging only the conversion of witness into 92 ter witnesses of witnesses number 117, 123, and 132. So these are not amongst them. Do I take it that we have the consensus of the Defence teams to grant the Prosecution motion or submission in relation to these six witnesses; namely, towit to convert them into 92 ter witnesses? Mr. Haynes, I think you're the one who was the spokesman on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I know from speaking to others that amongst the three witnesses who are due to testify today there may be some opposition to the receipt into evidence of information reports. And I don't wish to embarrass anyone, but that's a position I know Ms. Nikolic will take. So I can relay that to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But that is another matter, and I think for the time being the matter in issue is whether this is opposition to convert them into 92 ter witnesses. The documents will surface and come up in turn in the course of the testimony. Yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honours. The position is the same as presented by Mr. Haynes. But I have to address the Chamber concerning Witness 158. The Prosecution made a request on the 28th of February, but they didn't provide an accompanying 92 ter statement. We are now working on the basis of an informative report, which we see as a document under Rule 70. We believe that 92 ter cannot be applied in this case as the basis for admitting into evidence this informative report or information report created by an investigator of the OTP. The position of the Defence is should 92 ter be applied in relation to this witness and all other witnesses, then the OTP should have provided an accompanying proper statement signed by the witness or a transcript of the testimony as provided by Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who is dealing with this on the Prosecution side? Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can respond to that, if I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I thank my colleagues had the courtesy to tell me earlier that they were going to raise this issue. They called us late last night. I agree that an information report is not a witness statement. It is a different animal. However, in this case, I think the process that has been gone through with the witness has made it such that the information report functionally within Rule 92 ter is a statement. That there is no real difference. And the reason for that is as follows: The 92 ter statement, which we are using, the information report, reads very much like a witness statement. It contains the information that the witness gave to investigators during an interview. Now, yesterday I met the witness for the first time, and he then was given the opportunity to review the entire information report, verbatim, in his own language. He had to -- it read back to him, which is the only real difference between an information report and a statement, is that the witness has the information read back to him and says that's correct and signs it. That happened yesterday. It's a short, I think, three or four-page document. He read the translation. He made five minor corrections, and he said other than these five corrections it is accurate. Everything that is in this information report is what I said. And I explained the 92 ter process to him, that he would be asked if everything in the -- what he -- in the report was accurate, if it's what he was said, and if he would say the same things today. And he understood that and agreed with the proviso of the five minor corrections he had made. So the only difference between this and a formal witness statement is that it is not actually signed, although he has affirmed that it is correct. He has adopted it, he affirmed it is correct, he is going to swear under oath that he has read it and that his answers would be the same today. And if the only difference is the signature, he can read it again on stand and sign on the bottom. So I think that it's really a very minor technical difference between this report and a statement, and we're just trying to move things a little bit more quickly by -- by putting in this information report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls, it's an acknowledgment at the same time that Ms. Nikolic's submission, legal submission is correct; and as I read you, it's not something that has dawned on you today. You -- you were fully aware all the time that the information report is not the same as a statement for the purpose of Rule 92 ter. I do understand that you are trying to take a pragmatic, practical approach. At the same time, this pragmatic, practical approach is causing us to lose time, to waste time. Next thing I expect is someone to stand up from the Defence team and says we haven't had a copy of this statement now and we want time to go through it. It's -- it's procedure of inviting trouble, asking for trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I can just address that one point. The -- there should be no problem with notice, because the -- the report which they've read was disclosed over a year ago to -- to the Defence, and nothing has changed in it. He's read it. The only different -- and it's been translated. The only difference are quite minor corrections that he has made and those were sent to the Defence after I met with him yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would just like to point out two or three things. We are aware that an information report is a product of the work of the Prosecution. It's written in the third person. I can say it contains a summary of what the witness said. The witness did not read it immediately after it was drafted; he read it two years later. A statement can be used to refresh the witness's memory in cross-examination, and to confront him, but I believe that it's not fair, and it would not be correct to act according to Rule 92 ter on the basis of a report drafted by the Prosecution. This witness was supposed to be under 92 bis, and then at the request of the Defence, Witness 158 was withdrawn because there was no statement of that witness as the time. So they transferred him to the viva voce witness list; but on the 28th of February, in the request for conversion from 92 bis to 92 ter, this witness was then transferred and then we were told that we would be getting his statement within a reasonable amount of time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me suggest we take also a practical approach, pragmatic approach to this. He is not the first witness to come along, anyway he is the second. So we'll start with the first one who is 156. Is there any objection to the conversion of Witness 156 to a 92 ter witness? There is none. In the meantime, I trust that between today and tomorrow, when supposedly -- he's probably going to testify today as well. Between now and when 158 comes along, you will try to reach an agreement. You now do have a signed statement; and perhaps if the difference is not material and if it doesn't stand in the way, perhaps you can reach an agreement. Are there any objections in relation to the other witnesses, 124, 48, 168, and 16?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So authorisation is being given to convert these five witnesses into 92 ter witnesses. We'll hang around, and we will tell you what our decision is in relation to the next witness, 158. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can we go into private session for one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We appeal to you to sit down during the first break and try to sort matters out in relation to Witness 158. In the meantime, let's bring in Witness 156, please. Yes, Mr. Meek. Wait one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes. We would be happy to. I have some documents I want to tender through the cross-examination of Haglund. We can do it after the break. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think we'll do that together. I mean I understood there would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- documents, but since we haven't finished the Prosecution -- yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just on this same subject, you may recall, when Eileen Gilleece testified, we were speaking to Mr. Haynes about the statement or her information report on General Pandurevic's statement. Mr. Vanderpuye is handling that. He will be here after -- he'll be the third person, if we could deal with that issue Mr. Vanderpuye comes because we have been speaking to Mr. Haynes, and I think we'll need to have -- that will probably have to take some court time to deal with it because we haven't had an agreement on it. Perhaps we will by the time Mr. Vanderpuye is here, but that's just another matter that's hanging out there that we have to deal it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Dr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. You are about to start giving evidence. Before you do so, Madam Usher is going to hand you the text of a solemn declaration which you are required to make, undertaking that you will be testifying the truth. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Doctor. Please take a seat and make yourself comfortable. I don't think you will be here for a long time testifying. Mr. Thayer will go first. He will then be followed by the various Defence teams on cross-examination. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Could you please state your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Radivoje Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just briefly, sir, what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a general surgeon, and I work at the surgical ward at the hospital in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, Doctor. Do you recall giving a witness statement to OTP investigators in 2003?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, as I understand it, at the time a written translation was not prepared, so it was simply translated back to you in your own language from the English document. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And at the time I insisted that the statement be written in my mother tongue, in Serbian, so that I could directly read it and sign it. I believe that this was technically possible, because an interpreter was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, yesterday in my office did you, in fact, read a written translation of your statement in your own language?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I had the opportunity to read my statement in Serbian for the first time; meaning the translation from the English. And with minor corrections, there aren't too many of them, but which I believed were important, I agree with the statement, and that I gave it in 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And, Doctor, we will awe talk about some of those corrections or clarifications in a moment, and I think you already partially answered my next question. Can you attest, Doctor, before the Trial Chamber that other than the clarifications that we will talk about, that witness statement is true and accurate to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you further attest that if you were asked those same questions here in court, that your answers would be the same?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Doctor, what I'd like to do now is simply read for the Trial Chamber, a summary of your witness statement. It's not too long. And then after that we'll talk about some of the clarifications. Okay? The witness was born in 1959 in Kiseljak, Zvornik municipality. He identifies himself as Serbian. He is a surgeon at the Zvornik Medical Health Facility, where he has worked since 1985. In July 1995 he was working as a surgeon in the hospital's surgical ward. On a date, he cannot remember, in 1995, wounded Muslim males were brought from Milici by Dr. Jugoslav Gavric. He did not witness their arrival, but he knows they were placed in the hospital's gynaecology ward. He thinks that there were 11 Muslim patients. One of them had severe facial injuries and died at their hospital. The other patients' health was such that their lives were not in danger. Each of the patients was identified by name and had a treatment history written on his release form from the Milici hospital. They opened treatment history files for these patients at the Zvornik hospital. While at the Zvornik hospital, they were all provided with adequate treatment. The witness does not know how long they stayed at the Zvornik hospital, but he is convinced that it was more than one day. He does not know where the documentation related to the treatment of these patients is located. Dr. Lazarevic, Chief of Surgery, arranged around-the-clock security for these patients to prevent anyone besides medical staff from entering their rooms. The witness thinks they were guarded by policemen, but is not sure and cannot recall their uniforms. These patients were taken to the "Standard" military barracks at Karakaj, which was a shoe factory before the war. He does not know who gave the order to remove them from the Zvornik hospital to the "Standard" base, but supposes that Dr. Lazarevic was the one who received the order to do so. The witness and other doctors from the Zvornik hospital continued to treat the patients daily after they were transferred to "Standard." He personally treated them only once at "Standard," and they were accommodated in one big room separate from the wounded Serb soldiers. The second time he went to "Standard" to treat these patients he entered the room in which they had been accommodated but did not see them there. On that occasion a soldier told him that the patients were to be exchanged near Bijeljina. He does not know on what day or date that these patients were taken from "Standard." He did not notice any other Muslims at "Standard" on those two occasions. He is quite sure that in all of 1995 there were no other Muslim patients admitted and hospitalised in the surgery ward at the Zvornik hospital. He recalls twice providing first aid to Muslim prisoners. Both times the prisoners were escorted to the hospital by VRS soldiers, but none of them was admitted. After he gave the prisoners first aid, the soldiers took them to "Standard." The witness was shown documents bearing ERN numbers 0118-0281, 0118-0282, 0118-0285, 0118-0286, and 0118-0340. He recognised his handwriting, signature, stamp, and description of diagnosis and treatment at entry number 4582, indicating patient Azem Bajramovic. He does not recall this patient. His reference to "Standard" in this entry indicates that the patient was taken by the army to the "Standard" base. Regarding entry 4605, indicating patient "Fahro, son of Meho," the handwriting looks like Dr. Lazarevic's. The witness is sure that he did not treat this patient and has no knowledge of him. Finally, he recognised his handwriting and signature at entries 4904 and 4905, indicating patients Halid Alic and Hasan Alic. He recalls these patients looking miserable and dirty and that their wounds had not been treated so that the one had worms in the wound on his hand. After receiving first aid at the Zvornik hospital, they were taken by the military to "Standard." Although their health condition qualified them to stay in the hospital, the soldiers told him that the prisoners would be exchanged soon. Now, Doctor, there were some corrections and clarifications that you brought to my attention, so let's go through them, if we may. And I'll be referring to the different numbered parts of the statement, for ease of reference in the record. Doctor, as to part one, you told me that you were not present when the patients from the Milici hospital arrived at or left the Zvornik hospital. So you did not see these events yourself. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. My colleague referred to part one of the statement. It might be paragraph one to the notes that he provided us this morning, but I believe it has to do with part two of the statement. This -- once this witness will have terminated, Mr. President, we will have some observations to make; because under 92 ter, we should have a statement that the witness says what is there is good. Now we're making corrections to the statement, but I will keep that for after. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Go ahead. I'm not sure -- yes, the reply to the previous question is on the record. So your next question, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I do stand corrected with respect to the citation. It is part two of the statement, which does not -- is not numbered by paragraphs; it's just numbered by sections.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So, Doctor, let me repeat the question, just so we can move along. As to that part two, you told me that you were not present when the patients from the Milici hospital arrived at or left the Zvornik hospital, so you did not actually see those events. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. And I also noted -- I see my statement in English here, I don't see the Serbian translation, but I recall saying that I remember well that Dr. Jugoslav brought these patients and that I was not present. I was not present at the time they were brought to the hospital, and I was not present when they were taken away. There is no logic to that. This might indicate as if I was an eye-witness or that I have information from somebody. I did not see them coming to the hospital and I was not there. I did not see them leaving the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I think that's sufficiently clear now, sir. Now, Doctor, you also told me as to part three of your statement, that you don't know for certain if there was an order, in fact, to transfer the patients from the Milici hospital to the Zvornik hospital. Do you remember telling me that?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I said that, and I would like to repeat that. I didn't know then, I didn't know who had decided that they should come or that they should leave. I had no information about an order or a decision that these patients would be brought for treatment to us. As for Dr. Lazarevic, I just assumed that he would be able to know more information because the conversation with me lasted several hours. That interview was then made into a statement, and I said that perhaps Dr. Lazarevic would know the conditions or the circumstances in which the patients were brought to the hospital and taken away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like to know what -- whether my colleague is now correcting the statement or obtaining further clarification. This morning we received -- or yesterday we received notes concerning the proofing of this witness, with the number of information and the five or six paragraphs. My colleague just asked the witness to clarify whether he was there or not, when the -- they were -- the wounded Muslims arrived at the hospital. According to what I see in the statement, he already says, "I personally did not see their arrival, but I know that they were placed in a certain area." And later he says, "I cannot remember what day it was, after their departure, when they were taken from the hospital." I'm not sure if he is correcting any specific lines in the statement or whether he is filing the statement and doing as he did before, obtaining further information from the witness. Because that statement is going to go into evidence, so it is important to know whether what is in writing stays or doesn't stay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand what you are saying. On the other hand, you need to distinguish between the question and the answer. I mean, the question that was put to the witness was very specific. I mean -- and I don't know whether it really fits in what you have now raised. I mean, the question was: "Okay, I think that's sufficiently clear now, sir. Now, Doctor, you also told me as to part three of your statement, that you don't know for certain if there was an order, in fact, to transfer the patients from Milici hospital to the Zvornik hospital. Do you remember telling me that?" That was the question, and then we have an answer that goes for nine -- nine lines. So...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we rule on this, if it is a ruling at all, do you wish to state anything in regard to this, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, simply that I'm really trying to address very specific items that the witness brought to my attention, that he wished to in no uncertain terms to have clarified in order for him to attest to that statement. And I think this is a practice that we have adopted in the past, and I think it's worked well. I just leave it there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And apart from what we stated, or I stated earlier on, and I thank you for your response as well, Mr. Thayer, this is perfectly in line with what we decided in the first place in relation to the application of Rule 92 ter. I mean, the idea is to, as much as possible, streamline the procedure with the understanding that after the summary of the statement, there will be questions to add, to clarify. I mean, it's -- so let's move ahead, please. Mr. Thayer. Again, I don't want you to lose track. Your question was very specific, and it elicited a yes or a no answer. At the time the witness did go into detail. I honestly don't know what -- what the next question you had in mind was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think he sufficiently answered it in those nine lines, so I'll move on to my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, as to part four of the statement, you told me that you cannot say that you are quite sure that there were no other Muslim patients at the surgery ward of the hospital in 1995, as is written in your statement. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what you told me is that you can say that you think that there were no other Muslim patients treated there in 1995 other than the Milici Hospital patients and a few Muslims who were treated in your emergency room. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The question is not clear to me. What do you mean treated in the emergency room? There is no emergency room. These were patients who were brought to the urgent department, and then we would be treating these patients as in-patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you for that clarification. So with that clarification, Doctor, do you recall the question I just asked you about you now say that you think that there were no other Muslim patients treated in your hospital in 1995, other than the Milici patients and some others who were treated in-patient?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And, finally, just two other points that you brought up. As to part seven, you said that you did not remember the two patients' names at first during your 2003 interview; but after reading their entries in the emergency room protocol, you recalled their specific wounds and treatment.

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: In my statement it is not correctly stated. That's why I asked that it be corrected; namely, that I remember the patients well, and their names. I especially do not remember their names. However, the protocol that was put to me after analysing that protocol, I was able to establish that it was my handwriting, that I treated those patients. And based on their diagnosis, and the findings that I wrote down, I remembered that those were two patients who had been brought in as prisoners. They were brought to the surgical ward, or rather, to the department for urgent treatment. In addition to that, I wish to say that in the statement it says that they were not treated, but that's not true. They received proper treatment pursuant to the principles of war surgical rules. They were treated in the same way as our wounded. They were treated as out-patient clinics -- patients. And I said at the time that due to the fact that their wounds were neglected and in bad shape, they needed to be hospitalised, but I said -- I was told that that was not possible and that they needed to be exchanged. After they received surgical treatment, they were taken away by two soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the last correction that you brought to my attention, sir, was that you do not recall saying that the soldiers told you that the patients would be exchanged soon, only that they would be exchanged. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: That they were going to be exchanged, without "soon."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, what I'd like to do is just spend a little bit of time asking you a couple of questions to elicit some more detail that perhaps was missed in your interview in 2003. And, first, I just want to talk about these last patients that -- that you were just discussing. Do you recall whether you received any information as to where those two soldiers had been captured?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I did not receive any information.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And I'm not referring to a particular town, I'm just asking, did you receive any information about the circumstances of -- of the environment in which they were captured?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No information whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you just referred to being told that these two patients were not going to be admitted. Who told you that, that those two patients had to go to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: It is the doctors who decide on who is going to be admitted or not. I was the one who suggested that they be admitted, and those who escorted them there said that they were to be exchanged and could not be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And when you refer to those who escorted, you are referring just to some VRS soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I said two soldiers, as far as I could remember. Two soldiers escorted these two wounded men.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you recalled in your -- in your witness statement that we -- that we just heard the summary of, that 11 patients from Milici arrived with treatment histories and release forms from that hospital. And yesterday I showed you 11 sets of patient history and discharge records. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, did you have an opportunity to examine those records?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I only had occasion to see the discharge letter for all of the patients. Head of the surgical ward, Dr. Lazarevic, at the morning meeting, told us that those patients from Milici had been admitted, that they were going to be exchanged, and until that happened they would be treated in our ward. I personally saw these discharge letters, based on which we opened medical histories for them, medical history files, and continued the treatment that had already been initiated.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to ask you just one question about the actual records. After you reviewed the 11 sets of records which I showed you yesterday, were you able to draw any conclusions as to whom the 11 sets of patient history and discharge records I showed you yesterday are related?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The situation is quite clear in that regard. Based on the words uttered by the Chief, Dr. Lazarevic, about those people being admitted and being from Milici, and based on review of discharge letters signed by the doctors from the Milici Hospital, there was no doubt there. Those were the patients who had been brought to our hospital from Milici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could my colleague indicate to us which document he's talking about, give us a reference? Whether it is a document that was given to us, is it a new document, is it -- because I have a stack of documents. I cannot find hospital discharge records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's a fair comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm just getting there, Mr. President, that's my next step.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understood that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: With Madam Usher's assistance, I'm going to hand you copies, sir, of a packet of patient histories and discharge forms. This is 65 ter number 1884, and the English translation is ERN 0307-4271 through 4313, that's listed on our list of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, do you have -- do you still have a problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President. I have a list here of exhibits that were intended for this witness. This is a number that is not there. I'm told that it's a number that -- that is with another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may just respond briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like to see the documents so I can look at them, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I furnished, first of all, an e-mail to Defence counsel a couple of days ago with respect to adding this document, and it is on the most recent exhibit list, which I believe has been distributed via e-mail to Defence counsel. And it was also on the exhibit list for the next witness, Dr. Gavric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it clear now? Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, it's not very clear, Your Honours. I'm looking at a statement, witness -- this witness, and the description he just gave, 0307-4271 through 4313, or through -- yeah, it looks to me like B/C/S and he says English translation so...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am not in a position to confirm what correspondence was exchanged between the two sides. However, in the last witness Prosecution exhibit list that we have been given, under 65 ter number 1884, there is indeed a document dealing with 11 patient files of Muslim males were treated in the surgery ward of Sveti Nikola hospital in Milici on 13th, 14th, 1995, with ERN, last four digits, 4271 to 4313, and indication in what I have at least is that this is the English text. The corresponding B/C/S text would be -- would bear ERN numbers 6055 to 6133. I'm trying to help out. This is what I have. But, of course, if you have other indications, then please go ahead. I can't help you more than this.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's exactly correct, Mr. President. Those are the ERN numbers, the 65 ter numbers, and the description that was furnished to Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it all right now, Mr. Bourgon and Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Probably, because we have some -- we are probably confused with the number of e-mails we received and the number of lists we received. I did not imagine that these documents would be used with this witness. It's probably my mistake. I will need some time for cross-examination. These are three very simple witnesses, and now they are turning into a nightmare because we are using all kinds of different procedure with witness statements, with documents, with 92 ter. I don't know what -- what is happening, but there is for sure we will need time for cross-examination. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Doctor, you recalled in your statement that one of the patients arrived with severe facial injuries and, in fact, died during -- during his stay at your hospital. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were you able to identify, from that packet of records that is before you, someone whom you believed to be that patient that you referred to in your witness statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I don't intend to put this up in e-court and take up the time doing that. I'm just going ask him just to identify, and I will provide for the record the numbers for later on for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, with a great degree of certainty, that this is Aziz Becirevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. THE FRENCH INTERPRETER: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My attention is being drawn to whether there is a possibility to make it possible for the accused to be able to follow better.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In this case, Your Honour, I can provide the direct cites so the document that the doctor just referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we put them on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly. That is page 34 and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we have them in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We have them in e-court, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's bring them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's at page -- let's begin at page 34 of the English and page 60 of the B/C/S original of 65 ter 1884. And, with any luck, that's going to be the document. If -- and if -- is it possible to have the English posted as well, as long as we're doing it? It's page 34 of the English translation. It's not -- the English isn't in e-court? Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Doctor, having viewed this page, and I believe you answered my question, but we got a little side-tracked. I just want to ask you, is this one of the records which leads you to believe with a great degree of certainty, as you said, that the patient who died from his facial wounds is this individual, Aziz Becirevic?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We have the medical documents from Milici here. This is not the documentation from our hospital. Analysing these documents, I can say, with a great degree of certainty, that this is the patient in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Doctor. And we're done with that exhibit for now. Thank you. Now, lastly, yesterday in my office, I also showed you a -- a large document, and this is 65 ter number 1891. And, again, with Madam Usher's assistance I'll just hand this over to you. And I just ask you, Doctor, do you recognise what that document is?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: This is the protocol from the urgent medical service.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, during your interview in 2003, you were shown some photocopies from that document, some entries for four Muslim patients who were treated at -- at your hospital in July of 1995, and I just want to ask you a couple of follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, again, I'll need Madam Usher's assistance with the ELMO with this document. I understand it is in e-court. It will probably be easier all around to work with the ELMO because the graphs go from one page to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Doctor, if you would, there is a yellow tab marked tab number one, and I just ask you to place that open underneath the ELMO. And let's focus on the top half of that, and that's at ERN 0118-0281.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that there is a problem with this exhibit because if we follow the e-court, we have a document under that number that's only two pages, and the page that the Prosecutor just indicated does not exist in the e-court. I don't know if this is a new exhibit or is it an exhibit that obtained a new 65 ter number or maybe -- maybe it's a technical omission on behalf of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't help you there. Mr. Thayer perhaps can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, this -- this entire -- I believe, this entire exhibit has -- has been admitted. It was my understanding it was uploaded into e-court. In -- in any event, if it's not in e-court -- I'm being told it is in e-court, and I can -- I can provide the e-court page numbers for everybody's ease of reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have it in front of me. 404 pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that would be 1891.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we are talking only of one page -- or two pages, one in English -- sorry, two pages, 0285 to 0286, at the moment for the purposes of this testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, we will be referring to about eight pages in total during the course of his -- his testimony, and I will identify for the record by ERN and by e-court. And, Your Honour, I'm perfectly happy to do it in e-court, if it seems to be the consensus among my learned friends. And we can certainly proceed that way and perhaps alleviate some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I noticed you standing for a moment, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, Your Honours. Maybe my learned colleague could point out the page on the English translation as well to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do have English translations. One of the reasons I'm proceeding in this manner is they are frankly very, very poor, and what I'm going to do is ask the doctor to translate the entries directly from the B/C/S. Most of the -- because it's a hospital logbook, most of the entries were frankly illegible to the eyes of our translators. So that is why I'm proceeding in this way, just from the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau, I noticed you standing for...

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. President, I think it's a technical problem because we don't have access to this document. In fact, we don't even have access to 1891. We only have access to document 1891B, which is only composed of two pages.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If I may, for the record, the document is in e-court. It was submitted with another witness on the 16th of February as 1DP01891 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me try to direct you as much as I can. In the list of exhibits, the latest one, the most recent one, there are two 1891; one is 1891, and that's the second or the third document, and that's the Zvornik Hospital medical logbook. I take in its entirety from 1882 to 1930 in English, and then from 0007 to 0410 in B/C/S. That's one document. And that's in e-court and it should have been -- be available to all of you. If it's available to us, I think -- I suppose it's available to everyone. Then you are right, we do then have 1891B, which, to me, is two pages from that document only in B/C/S. What we have here indicated or listed is those due pages in B/C/S. And that's, as I understand it, is what Mr. Thayer is taking use of now. Correct me if I'm wrong, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was with you up to that very last part. What I'm showing the witness now is a previous page, one of the ranges that was listed at the first 1891 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- listing there. I think everybody can see that I have identified one, two, three, four, five, six page ranges that I had wished to show Dr. Novakovic. That's where we are now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Can Madam Usher bring down the document a little bit so we can see the ERN number? So we are talking of 0118-0281.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's exactly correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Is that clear now? All right. Yes, I see both of you standing. I understand Ms. Fauveau only wanted to say it's clear. Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Very briefly, could my colleague tell me what page the English translation is that he's referring to the document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: With the Court's indulgence, I'll just pull that out. That should be page 17 of the English translation, and we are focusing at the moment at entry 4578. And, again, I'm afraid the English translation isn't going to be much help because it's mostly listed at illegible, but that's the page number in the English translation. May I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Doctor, do you see the entry 4579? I believe it's the second entry from the top, on the -- on the right-hand page?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: 45 -- could you please repeat the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sure. It's 4579. The second entry down from the top of that page.

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you see a date --

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- written in there, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 14th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you just tell the Trial Chamber who was responsible for recording the dates in this logbook?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The information on the left is written in by a nurse, a medical technician.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was there any particular procedure that the nurses were required to follow in terms of when they wrote in the date in this logbook, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have the document before me in English, and I look at 4579 where my colleague is drawing the attention of the witness. I try to compare the log that I have there, and it has information with the date of 14 July and some kind of a name. I look at the English translation, I see "Jankovic", and I see "1929." The two just don't match. Either it is the wrong translation or it is a wrong document, but something is not working, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think it's time for the break. Mr. Thayer and his assistant will clear this up for you when we reconvene in 25 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer. Have you sorted it out?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I believe we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's great news. I mean about the first piece of good news this morning. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think what we're going to do, Your Honour, is use the e-court system, and I have identified the English pages for those of my colleagues. I think that were having some difficulties, which, as I said are understandable. The root of the problem is the legibility of the translation that has created this mischief. But I think we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I still see Mr. Bourgon on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I do not believe that the matter is resolved in the sense -- in the following sense: My colleague indicated to us previously that he was referring to page 17 in the English version under a serial number that applies to an individual, and that number was 4579.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And 4579 on page 17 in English does not match what we find in the B/C/S at 4579, different names and the date is not there. My colleague came to us at said at the break, and said, No, you have to look at page 21 which also has the number 4579. So the English version of this document is incorrect. And I think my colleague would acknowledge the fact that the English translation is not correct. Now, the matter is that we were informed only yesterday afternoon that this witness would even be questioned on this record. Plus, the mistake that happens with this, the mistake in the translation, make it that we have not been able to prepare appropriately for the testimony of the witness. I'm willing, of course, in order to make things proceed, to have the examination-in-chief to proceed today, but for sure I will be asking for a delay in order for me to study these records line by line. Mr. President, it must be brought into perspective here that these three witnesses were non-contentious witnesses. And if the Prosecution stuck with the information provided to us, either in the information statement or in the witness statement, there would be no problems. But just before they come, two years after -- more than two years after these witnesses were met, we come and we change the complete theory of the case as to what they want to do with those three witnesses. We're also going way further than what was announced in the Rule 65 ter summary. There is a ruling in other Chambers that when you have a Rule 65 ter summary, the Prosecution must stick to the Rule 65 ter summary. They are not sticking to the Rule 65 ter summary, and they are going beyond that. So all this change of procedure all the time make it that it is difficult for us to keep up and to know exactly what the Prosecution intends to do with those three witnesses which appear benign and were non-contentious before the last few days. The last point, I would like to make, Mr. President, as I indicated at the beginning, I made an objection to the questions being asked by my colleague. What I was referring to was page 17 of the transcript, lines 4 to 6. I had understood, maybe by mistake, but what I understood was what the Prosecution was proceeding to do was to make corrections to the statement and not the normal procedure that this Chamber is used to of simply asking further information from the witness, and we've done that with all 92 ter witnesses. That was not the problem. But I understood from page 17, lines 4 to 6 that we were actually making corrections to the statement. Now, on this basis, of course, Mr. President, I will object to that statement being entered into evidence. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to the last point first, I don't think there is anything further that needs to be argued with respect to the Prosecution's position. We have adopted the practice here that we make corrections and we make clarifications. I think I distinguished both, and I think we have continued to follow that policy. With respect to my learned friend's previous arguments with respect to the 65 ter summaries, et cetera, I'll keep my comments as brief as I can, but I feel compelled to respond. First of all, this exhibit with which we are working now has been on this witness's exhibit list from the beginning; this is Exhibit 1891. This is no surprise. This is an exhibit, selections of which were identified in his signed witness statement, which my colleagues have had for goodness knows how long, by ERN number. This is absolutely no surprise. There is no change of theory. There has never been any change of theory, I would submit, at all. Secondly, if one takes a look at the 65 ter summary, it is eminently clear that the topic of this witness's testimony has to do with these 11 Milici patients. Those are precisely the records which I showed this witness and about which I did advise Defence counsel within the last 48 hours or so. So there is no surprise here. They -- it cannot be credibly argued that anybody is being changed in terms of what their expectations are of this witness's testimony. It is all in the statements, it is in the summaries, it could not frankly be clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have one question on this. Earlier on I had asked Madam Usher to bring down a little bit the document which we had on the ELMO at the time, and you said that you were basically referring to about six pages, a block of six pages from that patient log. Can you repeat again the numbers, the ERN number of those six pages, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. Those ranges are 0118-0281 to 0118-0282, and then 0118-0285 to 0118-0286. I will also be showing 0118-0337, and then 0118-0339 to 0118-0341.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Carry on, if you have anything else to state.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Nothing, Mr. President. If I may continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So before we proceed, I think we have to draw a line somewhere. We do not entertain, in the least, or agree in the least, rather, with your submission that it is not regular, procedurally correct, for the Prosecution to ask questions or elicit answers from a witness that tend to correct the statement that he would, or she would have -- is being referred to. Your submission, Mr. Bourgon, would be tantamount to the following argument, which is untenable: Namely, that if, in asking the witness to attest that the written statement or transcript accurately reflects his declaration and what the witness would say if examined, if he departs just one little bit from his previous statement, then the conclusion, according to you, would be that that statement would therefore not be able to be tendered under Rule 92 ter. It would defeat the whole purpose of the Rule 92 ter procedure. The idea is it's divided into two parts. First, that the statement accurately reflects the witness's declaration. Secondly, whether it would also amount to what he would say if examined. We made it clear that there should be, and we expect, to be questions if, in being referred to his previous statement, the witness notices some things that need clarification and other things that maybe are not 100 per cent correct and need to be corrected. So that's number one. As regards the difficulty that you propose, if met in preparation, in being -- in preparing for the cross-examination, when you look at the witness's statement that is being referred to on page 4 - that's part 5, last paragraph in part 5 - is specifically being referred to the patient log and specifically to the pages that the Prosecution has just repeated to us on my prompt; the exception of 337 -- 8337 and 341, which are just two pages. If we see that there is a justification on the basis of those two pages to delay your cross-examination, we will not be unreasonable, but we expect you also not to be unreasonable. So let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may have page 275 of 65 ter 1891 displayed in e-court, please. That is page 21 of the English translation, and with any luck it will be ERN 0118-0281. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I believe where we left off, I had asked you whose responsibility it was to enter the date into this logbook.

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: To repeat, I said that a doctor is not supposed to do that. A nurse or a medical technician is supposed to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was there a particular procedure that the nurse or medical technician was supposed to follow in terms of when they were supposed to enter the date into the logbook?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: There was the regular procedure; a nurse is supposed to enter the particulars that are on the left-hand side of the protocol.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And those particulars would include patient information, place of birth, date of birth, and their name; is that correct, as we see it here before us at 0281?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You can see that, at the top of the logbook, what the page is supposed to contain.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So let me ask you again, Doctor, with respect simply to entering the dates into the logbook, was there a particular procedure that the nurse or medical technician was supposed to follow as to when the date was entered into the logbook?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The period between two dates refers to the period of 24 hours. So here under 579 you have the date, the 14th of July, 1995. If then on some other page it's the 15th of July, then that would refer to a 24-hour period. That's how it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, if we could please just scroll down just a tad, please. And do you see the entry at 4582, sir? I believe it's circled?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you please just read what has been entered there into the record?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: It says, "Azim Bajramovic, born in 1954." Then it's not clear what it says. "Dobrok Skelani," but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: And then it says "11.00," if you can see it, meaning that the patient was examined in the morning on the 14th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this is a logbook that actually continues horizontally to the subsequent page.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So if I could ask -- ask Madam Usher's assistance, simply to scroll horizontally to the next page, and if we can maintain, maybe if we can do a split screen with the following page, which would be page 276, and just put them side by side, so we can...

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, we're looking at ERN ending in 0282 here. Do you see your handwriting anywhere for an entry? And, again, this is still page 21 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the top the fifth one refers to patient Azim Bajramovic. "Vulnus scloptarium darso-coli." That is my handwriting. I treated the patient. I don't recall the particulars, but it says in Cyrillic, "primarily surgical treatment of the wound" and "Standard," and there is my signature in Cyrillic. So I treated that patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what does the reference to "Standard" mean there?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: In order to continue his treatment, he was sent to the medical ward of the Karakaj barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Doctor, is it fair to say that the entries that are on the right-hand side of the logbook are either filled in by the doctor or dictated by the doctor?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we could have page 279 of the document in e-court, please, and this is page 22 of the English translation, and this should appear as ERN 0118-0285. There we have it. And if we could please scroll down and focus on the bottom half of the document. That's perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you see entry 4605, sir? Where it says, "Fahro, son of Meho." Do you see that entry, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you just read the rest of that entry there, please?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: It's illegible. I didn't write that. I can try. It says for the column for the year of birth, one nine, so the date of birth is incomplete; and then it should say Srebrenica in the next column, but I'm not sure. And the time, 000 hours on the 15th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we look directly below that entry at 4606, do you see a date, in fact, has been written in, sir; and if so, can you just read what that says?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The date is the 15th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we may have --

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: And this is under the name Momir Kresanovic. I'm not sure, born in 1964; Brnjica VP; military post, 7469; Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may have page 280 of the document in e-court please, and that's page 22 of the English translation. And if we could scroll over -- or scroll down, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Doctor, do you see the third entry up from the bottom, which should correspond with the entry at 4605? Do you see that third entry up from the bottom?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see the number, but I do see the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recognise the handwriting that is along that row there, third up from the bottom? Do you think you know whose handwriting that is, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I can state responsibly that it's not my handwriting, but it could possibly be the handwriting of Dr. Lazarevic. I'm not sure but it could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Doctor, there appears to be some Latin written in there. If you would, could you just translate using your medical knowledge what that is, if you can read it?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: "Vulnus sclopetarium brachi dex et genus sin." Translated it means that the injury is inflicted with a fire-arm in the area of the left upper arm -- right upper arm and left knee.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Doctor, are you able to make out the rest of the entry along that row?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: "Cleaning, processing, bandaging," and then the bottom is illegible. But I assume, since all wounds are treated in the same way, according to the principles of military surgery or war-time surgery, it could mean antibiotic and analgesic, and to the right it says, "AT protection." That's what's there. We probably did write a report. There would be a report by the surgeon, which would be sent to the doctor who referred the patient or to whom the patient was being sent for continued treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Doctor, you just referred to "AT" something. Can you just tell us what that means? You used the abbreviation "AT". Just wondering what that abbreviation means.

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: "Anti-tetanus protection," meaning that it's protection against the wound getting infected.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, may we have page 331 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: May it please the Trial Chamber, could my colleague just clarify that nothing in the English translation that this witness has just testified from the B/C/S shows up in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's absolutely correct. It was all illegible to the eyes of the translators, and that's why we proceeded the way we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you can proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Great. We are at 0118-0337, if we may just focus on the bottom portion of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you see entry 4895? And this is page 41 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you see a date, Doctor, that is entered next to that entry for 4895?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The 24th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, may we have page 333 of this document, please, and that's page 42 of the document. And if we could scroll down, please. Thank you. Perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just my last set of questions, Doctor. Do you see the entries at 4904 and 4905?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you please just read into the record the information that's contained first at line 4905 and then at the entry for 4906, please. I'm sorry, 4904 and 4905, I apologise. So it's 4904 and 4905.

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The names are illegible, so I'm not sure, because I didn't write that myself. I'm not sure if I'm going to read it correctly. Should I read it? Try to read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Give it a shot, Doctor, please.

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Under number 4904, it's possible that it says "Alic," I can't read the name. The year of birth, "1967," and this could be Srebrenica. I'm not sure. It's illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the entry below it, 4905?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: "Alic Hasan," it's possible. Year of birth, "1969." And, again, it's the same as the writing above, so it could be "Srebrenica."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And if we may move to the next page, 334 in e-court, and that should be ERN 0118-0340. And if we could scroll down and maintain those two rows.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see your handwriting, sir, in this portion of the document?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Third and fourth from the bottom is written in my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you just please read, and translate, the Latin to us, please, for those two lines.

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But before I do that, I complained about my statement because I didn't have a chance to translate that. It says in my statement that I was familiar with the cases and with the names. That is not true. I was given this logbook to look at. I was given it by the gentleman who interviewed me. And by looking at the logbook, I recognised the right side of this logbook, and I can state with full responsibility that this is my handwriting and that I treated these two Bosniaks.
