Diagnosis is "vulvus explosivum antebrachii dex," and then it says, "Cleaning the wound, debrievement [phoen]," and then it says, "Plaster on the upper arm" and then my signature. Do I need the translate the diagnosis for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Whatever that Latin meant, sir, if there is a colloquial term, that would be fine?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Explosive injury to the right upper arm with fracture of the bone, and then the kind of treatment; and then it says that the patient was sent to Standard. And then below, "vulnus explosivus femoris sin capiti dex et dig II et III manus sin." "Cleaning the wound and debrievement, which is to say explosive injury. The one inflicted by mines and explosives on the left thigh, right knee, and the second and third finger of the left hand, and then the kind of treatment received; and then it says that the patient was sent to Standard. These are the patients who were prisoners, who were brought as prisoners, and I explained in my statement the circumstances. These wounds were quite neglected. These were recently captured Bosniaks. I treated them, and I said that due to their wounds they should be hospitalised. But the soldiers said that they had to be exchanged, and they were taken out of the surgical ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, lastly, doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may have page 335 of the document in e-court, please, and that's still at page 42 of the English translation. And if we could just scroll down a little bit, a little bit more. That's good, perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see the entry at 4912, doctor?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you see a date next to that entry; and if so, can you just read into the record what it says?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. "The 25th of July, 1995."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. That concludes my direct. I thank you, and I appreciate your patience during these technical difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Thayer. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Zoran Zivanovic. I defend Mr. Popovic in this case. I would like to put several questions to you precisely in relation to your statement. You told us that upon giving the statement to the OTP investigators, you asked to receive a written translation, if I understood you well; a written translation of your statement, or rather, the translation into Serbian. Did you ask that immediately upon giving the statement, or was it done later?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: In 2003, as I've told you, following the interview which lasted for several hours, a statement was drafted in English. It was interpreted to me by the interpreter, and I was offered to sign. Initially, I protested. I refused to sign it. I asked that the statement be written down in my native language, Serbian, so that I can read it without an intermediary, and sign it then. I believed this to be technically possible because there was an interpreter there. However, my request was not granted; and despite that, I signed the statement as it was in 2003. The first time I had occasion to read that statement in my native language, in Serbian, was yesterday. It was in Serbian, and it was a translation from English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you given an explanation at the time as to why they didn't want to translate that statement into your native language and give it to you to read in written version?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the explanation that I was given was not a convincing one. They said that it wasn't typically done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look at the statement that you signed. It's in English; 1D209, or 52408 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 52480.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It will come up on the screen. Would you please look at page 5 of that statement, 0327-1160. I'm going to ask you to look at the handwritten portion, and your signature is right below it. Would you please tell me whether you wrote this down?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not write the text, but the signature is mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who wrote this text?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: It's possible that it was done by an interpreter, a lady interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it done after you had asked that the entire statement be translated to you in writing when you refused to sign it?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Following that, yes. I protested and initially I refused to sign the statement, but then after this I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of this statement we can see when it was taken, on the 6th of March, 2003. However, you told us just now that you gave that statement, or rather, that you were interviewed for a couple of hours. Do you remember exactly how long it took?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Two or three hours. The interview took that long. They put questions to me. It was of an informal nature. It was more than two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you present when the English text was drafted?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was present. The reason I signed it, ultimately, is that I have some knowledge of English. I don't speak it well enough, but I was able to understand the gist of the statement. I was told that the statement was not translated in the native language of the person interviewed, so I decided to sign it after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: After giving the statement, were you in touch with the OTP investigators? Did they call you again or ask you about something later on?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The first and formal contact was yesterday when the statement was put to me in the Serbian language, and that was the first time that I was able to read my statement in my native language.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And in the meantime you had no contacts with the OTP and their investigators. You had no occasion to repeat your request about the statement?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Who's going next? Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good morning, Doctor. How are you?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I just have a few questions on your original statement, and since it's already on the e-court, could we go back to page 0327-1157. And, Doctor, you have just indicated you have some knowledge of English, but perhaps not fluent. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's the wrong page. No, it's the right page. Scroll down so we can see number 2. Yeah, scroll up, whatever. I need to see number 2. There.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, Doctor, while you're looking at that, and I know you don't probably read English fluently. Am I correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Can I see the translation into Serbian, so that I can compare it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we have them both concurrently on the same screen? I think we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You see it, doctor?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In your proofing notes dated the 19th day of March, the OTP attorney Nelson Thayer, who just questioned you, indicated that during the proofing session, you provided some following information. Part of that was you stated with respect to part 2 of your original OTP statement given 6 March 2003 that you did not know for certain if there was an order to transfer the patients from the Milici Hospital to the Zvornik Hospital or if there was an order to transfer them from the Zvornik Hospital to the Standard barracks. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You then went ahead in your proofing notes to tell Mr. Thayer of the OTP that you don't think it was a hospital decision to bring these patients in or to transfer them out. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, would you --

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: That was my assumption. I wasn't an eye-witness. I wasn't a participant in the decision to bring them to the Zvornik Hospital. I worked there as a surgeon, and I didn't have any major competences there. I had my boss there to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And then would you agree with me, Doctor, that it very well could have been the hospital's decision to transfer them from Milici to Zvornik Hospital and thereafter to the Standard barracks? Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to speculate. There was a director there, a head of the ward, and they were in the know, so to speak. I have no information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. Well, I appreciate the fact that you don't want to speculate, but didn't you just speculate with the Office of the Prosecutor in your proofing session when you said that you didn't think it was the hospital's decision?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, what's the objection, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's been asked and answered, and at this point I don't see the relevance of asking this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I don't think it's been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please rephrase your question, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Doctor, just very simply, when you had a proofing session with the Prosecutor, Mr. Thayer there, on the 19th, yesterday, didn't you tell him that you don't know whether there was an order to transfer the patients from Milici to Zvornik Hospital or if there was an order to transfer them from Zvornik to the Standard barracks. And you went on to say, however, you don't think it was the hospital's decision to bring the patients or to transfer them. Correct? That's what you told Mr. Thayer yesterday, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I would disagree with you. I protested about the order to have them transferred. I didn't know at the time, and I don't know now, who decided on that issue; both to bring them to the Zvornik Hospital and to take them out of the hospital. As I've told you, I was a surgeon on the team, and other people made the decision and I have no information about it. No information whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And I appreciate that, Doctor. I'm just asking you simply, when you told the Prosecutor yesterday that you don't think it was the hospital's decision, that was speculation, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: An assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Again, looking at the statement, the very last page, page 5 which would be 0327-1160, which should be the signature page. I think you could put it up in the English version because there's handwritten B/C/S. Okay. There it is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In fact, Doctor, you didn't hand write the B/C/S portion that's underneath the typed, dated line of 6 March 2003, but you actually signed it underneath, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And doesn't that state that this -- your statement had been read to you in your own language and you understood it?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The statement was read to me by the interpreter in my language, but in addition to that, since I believed it to be technically possible, I asked that the statement be written to me in my own native Serbian language. However, that wasn't done. And the same happened with my other colleagues who gave statements. They all had to sign statements in English. So I state with full responsibility the signature underneath is mine and what's above it is mine, but I didn't write this text.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And did you indicate in your questions [sic] to my colleague, Mr. Zivanovic here, that you in a way upset with the way the OTP did the statement, took the statement from you?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The process of taking the statement did not upset me. It was a very proper kind of procedure, questions and answers; and then it was made into a written statement, which was in English. And when I was told to sign it, it was then that I got upset and I refused to sign it and I told you what I already said, namely that I wanted the statement to be provided in writing in my native language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yet you went ahead and signed it back in 6th of March, 2003, and then it wasn't until yesterday that you realised that the English version of your statement that you gave back in March of 2003 was wrong in several respects. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And didn't this upset you, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I simply stated that. I approved the major part of my statement, and then I had some corrections. There were some details that, in my view, were important and were misrepresented. Precisely because I did not have the statement in my native language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Are you sure those portions were misrepresented because you didn't have them in your native language or they were misrepresented by the OTP so that your statement would look more favourable for their case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You don't need to put an objection, raise an objection. Move to your next question, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Judge, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. [Microphone not activated] Who is going next? I had indications that the Pandurevic team wanted to cross-examine this witness. The Nikolic team too. The Miletic and Gvero team also. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we will not have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's take it in turns. Thank you, Madam Fauveau. Madam -- yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Likewise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Madam Nikolic or Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I am not ready at this time to proceed with my cross-examination, and I would ask for the -- the indulgence of the Trial Chamber. There is some verifications I need to do with the records, with the English version, compared with the B/C/S versions. There is the one specific issue I would like to raise concerning the people that were treated by the witness, and I need some time to go over these documents. I understand that you will not entertain what I suggested earlier concerning the fact that these documents were not referred to in the witness -- or were referred to in the witness statement; however I'm not ready at this time. What I suggest, Mr. President, we can proceed maybe with the other co-accused in this case, and hopefully with one break I could be ready to proceed; if not, I would ask the Court that the witness be recalled tomorrow morning and I would proceed very quickly for -- to terminate my cross-examination. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Borovcanin team have indicated that they do not wish to cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and we stick to this. We have no cross-examination for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That leaves also only the Pandurevic team, Mr. Haynes or Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: I will put several questions to you. The two patients that you spoke about, Alic Halim and Alic Hasan, you said about them that their wounds were neglected and that they were treated at the out-patient clinic and then taken to Standard. You were shown medical documentation, medical logbook, or the protocol, where the nature of the wounds is indicated, as well as the names of the patients. Based on that logbook, would you be able to establish when they were admitted?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: By analysing the logbook, above the names on the left side, where the second patient is recorded, it says, "14th of July, 1995." So if this is entered correctly by a nurse or a medical technician, it should be the 14th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Based on the logbook, would you be able to establish on which day they were taken to Standard?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: On the same day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Thayer, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the sake of making sure the record is clear, I think the -- I notice that the witness was looking at the open logbook on the ELMO, which, if I recall correctly, is open to an entry that does not relate to the two patients to whom my learned friend was just referring. So I just want to make that clear. And I can be corrected if that's wrong, but I just don't want there to be any lack of clarity in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's a fair comment. I think you need to address this, both of you, and the witness, so that we are clear as to what he's being referred to. Yes, Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: If I may assist the witness, it says here that Alic Halid is written down under 4904 and Hasan is 4905. I don't know if this is of assistance.

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Could this be shown to me, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I have the cites for that and we can return. That's page 33 -- well, if we're trying to establish the date, which I think I did with the witness, I can cite the page that actually has the date. If we're looking for the page which contains the entries for those two individuals, that's at page 333 in e-court, and, again, that's page 42 of the English. And those will be entries 4904 and 4905.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need to -- yes. Okay. Scroll it down. Yes. Okay. Thank you. What are we waiting for? All right. Have you found the reference, doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really can't find my way around this document that is being shown to me. 4005 [as interpreted], Alic, is that what it is? Can I also look at the right half of the logbook, if possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let him scroll with the original logbook.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: On the ELMO, Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Doctor, you can refer to the original logbook, which is on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Doctor. Doctor. Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it makes your life easier, what you are seeing on the screen, on the monitor, is a reproduction of what you have in the original patients' log to your right on the ELMO; the original book itself. Perhaps if you prefer, you can consult that and we can send you Madam Usher to assist you finding, locating the page. I think that will make things easier. Madam Usher, I think we're talking of page 333, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that document isn't numbered but I've numbered it as tab 6 on the yellow tabs. I think that will get us there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think let -- let the witness familiarise himself with the pages that he is being referred to first. If you wish to go through the pages in the original rather than concentrate on what you have on the monitor, then please do so, by all means. I'm talking to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it on the screen now. Alic Halid and Alic Hasan, and I have both the left and the right side of the logbook, so I can see it now. So if possible, could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Based on the documents here, can you be certain about the date when they were taken to Standard -- when they were treated and then taken to the Standard facility after being examined?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I already said that the left side of the logbook is something that the nurse or medical technician take care of, and then on the other side there are notes about the patients that I treated. So if there is a date, it would need to be on the left-hand side. I don't see it here. I don't remember the exact date when this happened. But I know, by looking at the logbook, that I was the one who treated these patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: If you looked at this document more carefully, would you be able to determine the date, looking on the left-hand side of the logbook?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: If it's a correctly registered logbook, then I could be able to tell. Perhaps if I saw the previous date on the left-hand side, I would be able to tell. On this part, on the left-hand side that I see now, I don't see any dates. So I would need to look at the date before and the date after, because, as I already said, this would refer to a 24-hour time period. That's how it should be, if the logbook was recorded correctly. But this is again something that is not part of a doctor's duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at the pages of the document based on which he could see the previous date and the date that is written after this? So that we could see which day it was. Perhaps -- this is probably a document that has the dates entered, so perhaps we can look for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I believe that's going to be at page 331 of e-court, page 41 of the English, and if I could ask the doctor to flip the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it will be easier if Madam Usher again assists the witness by referring him straight to the original that he -- he has on the ELMO, to page 331.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be easier for me to actually look at the logbook. It's in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown the protocol then, the logbook.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The previous page under number 48 -- actually, it's the third patient from the top, the date is the 24th of July, 1995. If this is correct, then it should be the 24th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. That is sufficient for now. I would now like to ask you to, on the page that has number 4904, if we can go back to that page, 4904, where Hasan and Halid Alic are registered. Would you agree with me, and you've already said that, mentioning their names, but previously when you were looking at the document you said that you could not be sure if it actually was Halid, if that was the name. Can we agree now that this is then about two persons, Hasan Alic and Halid Alic, under numbers 4904 and 4905?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't write that, but I assume that it could be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Well, you said that you assumed that because it was not your handwriting. Would you agree that under number 4904 there is the name Halid there?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: This H is a bit of a problem, but it's very probable that it is Halid.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you. It's not your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And it would be highly probable that this is Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now show the witness document which was handed in today. It's document -- it's a report on the decision by the Chamber for Human Rights on the register of the Batkovic collection centre, and could that document be placed on the ELMO, please. Let's look at page 7, please. Under number 6679, there is the name Alic Halid; Srebrenica; the 24th of July, 1995; and departure on the 12th of September, 1995; and the remark is, "Exchange." Do you agree that this is what is stated in this document, and Halid Alic's year of birth is marked at 1967?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: In the left-hand side of the logbook there is no date of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: No, no. 6679, you have the name Alic Halid?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. I apologise. I'm interested in the year of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: It says the 1st of January, 1967. This is the fifth column after the name of the father?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Under number 6680, there is the name Alic Hasan, father's name is Hamed; date of birth is 1969; also Srebrenica; the same date of arrival, the 24th of July, 1995; and date of departure is the 12th of September, 1995; and there is also the note there, "Exchange."

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says on the document on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Can we agree that this is a document with identical first names, last names, the year of birth, and the place of residence, as of those persons who are in the medical logbook under protocol number 4904 and 4905?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Looking at the logbook, then your assertion is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you. There is one more question. I would like to use your knowledge and the information that you have about the way people were treated who were brought in. I'm thinking of prisoners brought in by the Zvornik Brigade. Can you please tell me, if it was necessary to take an X-ray, if a fracture was suspected, where was this carried out?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: It was done at our hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: At the hospital. And outside of this, and I'm generally speaking about when the prisoners were brought in, so I'm not talking about specifically these two persons whose names we mentioned or the other names, I'm just generally speaking. If it was necessary to have an X-ray, these people would be brought to your hospital; and then the X-rays, would they return to wherever they came from with the X-rays?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: All the persons that were brought, I'm talking about prisoners, by anyone from the Zvornik Brigade for an examination or medical treatment to your hospital, were they treated identically as Serb wounded persons?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I assert that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: And these 11 persons, these prisoners who were taken from the hospital to Standard and who were treated adequately, is that -- does that apply to them?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. According to the principles of military medicines -- medicine, and they were treated in exactly the same way as the soldiers from our side were treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That basically brings --

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, excuse me. Just one more thing. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: A patient who died at the hospital who was not taken to Standard, would you agree that his name was Aziz Becirevic?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Looking at the medical documents that were shown to me from Milici, I can say with the highest degree of certainty, or probability that that is the same patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: I would like to ask...

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have document 7D169 shown to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is not in the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could go on a break a little earlier so that then we can find the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have -- we can do either of two things, either have the break now. In any case, we can send the witness out, that's for sure. The second thing is we can still have the break at 12.30, as scheduled. In the meantime we can dispose of the exhibit, Haglund exhibits, and also of the other issue that I raised with Mr. Bourgon earlier on about those three documents reminiscent of -- or of PW-101's testimony. I think the witness can be escorted out, and I don't see why we couldn't dispose of the Haglund exhibits issues first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Sarapa, we will continue with your cross-examination after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, you promised us that you would check the list and inform Mr. McCloskey if you had any objection to the introduction of any of those documents that he mentioned earlier on in relation to Dr. Haglund's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I talked with Mr. McCloskey at the break, and he indicated that the documents, additional documents he wished to introduce were P00612, 613, 614, 615, 617, 618, 619, 620, 623, 624, 625, which he indicated to me that because of the cross-examination by Mr. Haynes that these were mentioned. I don't believe they were mentioned. I believe there was a general question to Haglund about his record keeping but I don't believe those were mentioned, and I object to that, to any of those and all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Meek. Mr. McCloskey, can you respond to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think what I was referring to is I believe, and Mr. Haynes can correct me if I'm wrong, but I think Mr. Haynes was complimenting Dr. Haglund on his attachments because they were so complete with all this information. It's my understanding that's the information that is part of Dr. Haglund's report, that Mr. Haynes was talking about. I may be wrong, but that's what I was explaining to Mr. Meek. It's part of his report and part of the 94 bis application to the report. It didn't get on the 92 bis part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek. Do you wish to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's where I'm a little concerned. It's either it was in evidence or it's not in evidence, and now they want it to be in evidence because a single question that didn't mention any of these documents, so...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think, to be honest with you. I personally would like to postpone our decision because I am not informed sufficiently here and now of what the position is. We will go deeper into this, and I will come down with our decision later on if to admit these documents or to accept your objection. I'm not in a position to comment. I don't know if my colleagues are. But I think we will have to check the records to see what the position is before we jump. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I will agree, Judge. And if you want to take a break now, fine. Otherwise, I have five documents I would like to have tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you can safely move to that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, you can tender them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. Document 2D70 which was the report of the oversight committee of the San Antonio report, is what we referred to it as; 2D73, that was a document that was shown to Haglund. He was interviewed actually in that one. He was a moderator of a panel; 2D75, another article, "The Science of Human Rights," that was written by Jim Austin, and Dr. Haglund testified about that; 2D78, an article from the Human Rights Centre: "All That Remains Identifying The Victims of The Srebrenica Massacre," by Laurie Vollen, which was discussed on cross-examination; and 2D80, which would be the chapter 9 of the book, "The Key to My Neighbour's House," by Elizabeth Neuffer, which was specifically discussed, the excavations and exhumations done by Dr. Haglund back in 1995, 1996, in the area of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Does any other Defence team wish to tender any documents in relation to Dr. Haglund's testimony? None. Mr. Bourgon, those three documents used with PW-101, have you verified?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President, we verified. With the first two documents -- or sorry the last two documents, P311 and 1D217, one is a death certificate of the mother of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- of the chief of transportation. The second one was a -- an attendance record. Now, with regards to the first one, P295, this is a vehicle log, and my only difficulty is I only want to introduce in evidence the exact pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There were two pages. They are indicated. We don't have --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, so only those two pages, and yes, indeed, we would like to have those two pages admitted, and I believe my colleague did not object to those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So in conclusion on this issue and in relation to the testimony of PW-101, the three documents sought to be admitted by the Nikolic Defence team; namely, two pages, document P295, P311, and 1D217 are hereby being admitted, there being no objection on the part of the Prosecution. I think we will have the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Before we go for the break and before we decide, of course, on Mr. Meek's request or submission to tender his documents, is there an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we can decide it now. So your documents are being admitted. We will have a 25-minute break. Would that be sufficient for you, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed it will, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's deal first with the issue raised by Mr. Meek, responded to by Mr. McCloskey, in relation to those documents that the Prosecution seeks to tender with Dr. Haglund's testimony. You seem to mention, Mr. McCloskey, Rule 92 ter or Rule 94, nothing of the sort. Dr. Haglund testified and his reports were introduced under Rule 92 bis, and there is no other rule applicable. However, our position is that these annexes are part and parcel of his various reports and are necessary for a proper understanding and instruction of his evidence, and therefore they are so admitted. Now, have you sorted out, Mr. Sarapa, have you identified the -- all right. So we can proceed and conclude with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We have. All I wanted to add is that the document I used previously, which is the list of exchanged persons, already in the e-court under number 3D17; both in the original, in the Serbian language, and in English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Doctor, could you please tell me what procedure is applied if a patient dies?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean a typical procedure?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if there is a death on a ward, death signs have to be established. EKG is performed. They need to establish that there are no vital signs of life. The patient has to remain on the ward for two hours and after that he is taken to the morgue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Who informs of the death?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Your question is not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: When a patient dies in the hospital, who does the hospital inform of the death?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The doctor treating the patient has to write the fact of death in the medical history, then a death certificate is written and then the family is informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: When Aziz Becirevic died, do you remember what the procedure was for informing the family?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the procedure at all in that case. I am not aware of the fact when he died and where his body was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Did you have previously such cases where prisoners died at the hospital due to injuries?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, as far as I am aware that was the first and only case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If possible, could we see document 7D169? 7D169.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Here we see the date, the 16th, you can see the English translation, ERN 0308-9357. You can see in this document. This is the logbook of the person on duty. It says here that Aziz Becirevic died, and at the hospital, Dr. Novakovic notified that the utility company should take care of it. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't remember this, and typically doctors are not tasked with informing the utility company.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: The fact that it is not the duty of the doctor to inform the utility company to arrange the funeral, is that the reason that you informed?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: It says here that "Aziz Becirevic died at the hospital and that Dr. Novakovic notified the utility company should take care of it." Since it is not your duty to inform the utility company of the fact of the death, is this the reason why you informed the Zvornik Brigade, because it was your intention to inform the Zvornik Brigade so that they could contact the utility company?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that the Zvornik Brigade was informed. I don't even know who wrote this down. This is not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: This is not your document, and this is not your handwriting. This is a notebook belonging to the Zvornik Brigade; namely, it says there that the hospital reported that Becirevic had died and that utility company had been informed to arrange for the funeral?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that I reported this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: You don't remember?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. It is possible, but I don't remember that detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like to pick up where my colleague just left off concerning the wounded prisoner, Aziz Becirevic, that you were just discussing with my colleague. And I would like first to refer you to the document which my -- was used by my colleague, and that is 65 ter number 1884.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I have here the English, if I can have side by side the English and the B/C/S on the e-court. In English it is page 35, and in B/C/S I do not have the page number, but the ERN ends with 6132.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I believe that will be, depending on exactly which pages, either page 60 or page 61 of the B/C/S original of that document, 1884.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. On the right side I have the English version, and I'd like to have the same thing on the left side, but in B/C/S. I'm not sure we're talking about the same document. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Witness, looking at this document, you confirmed already that this is the person who died at the hospital. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: This portion of the discharge letter is not quite legible. I see Aziz Becirevic on the English version but not on the original. I can't tell whether the name is the same. I don't think it is the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You are correct, it is not the right page. Perhaps my colleague from the Prosecution can help us identifying the right page in the B/C/S, the right original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think that's page 60 or 61 of 1884 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. I believe, Witness, we have the right page now, and I would draw your attention to this document. So now the ERN number, just for the record, ends with 6115. So, first of all, Witness, I'm not sure you did answer the question. I will say it again. You confirm that this is the person who died after arriving at the Zvornik Hospital; the one of the wounded prisoners that were transported there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Looking at the document with a great deal of certainty, I can say that this is the patient, Aziz Becirevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if I look at this document in terms of the day he was admitted at -- now, this is the Milici Hospital, you confirmed that already. So at Milici Hospital he was admitted on the 13th and released on the 14th. Is that what this document says?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So if this -- if this person was transported along with the other prisoners on the 14th, that means that he would arrive at Zvornik Hospital sometime in the day on the 14th. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't an eye-witness, and I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you any idea at what time of the day the group of prisoners arrived on the 14th at Zvornik Hospital?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I draw your attention now to the bottom of this document, where it says, just before the signature line, that "the patient was transferred to Zvornik Hospital on the orders of the VRS chief of medical corps." Do you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: It says here on this discharge letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, do you know who Dr. Davidovic is?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And who is he?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: He is a neurosurgeon. He worked at the war hospital in Milici.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if we have his signature on this document, I take it we have no reason to doubt that the patients were transferred from Milici to Zvornik on the orders of the VRS chief of the medical corps. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The patients were transferred to the Zvornik Hospital. I wasn't present when that happened, and that's what it says here. I don't have any information as to why it is written here. It says here that this was done pursuant to the order of the chief of medical corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my question is simple: Do you have any reason to doubt that, looking at this document?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there shouldn't be any, because normally people are held liable for any forgeries, so this document should be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I'd like now to move to another document, which was shown to you by my colleague, and that is document 1891. That's the 65 ter number, and I have page 279 in B/C/S, and page 22 in English. Can we have those side by side on e-court, please. Witness, I draw your attention to the left side of the screen before you, and at the serial number 4605. My colleague showed you this document and you identified a name, which I cannot really read, and you said that he was from Srebrenica and would have been admitted at midnight on the 15th of July. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that; I read this out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just for the sake of clarification, if we're talking about midnight, it could mean different things depending on what day you're talking about, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you agree to that, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the document says 00 on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: To me it makes no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My question to you, sir, is about this patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if we can move to have the remainder of the page and that is, on the B/C/S side, we have to go to, I guess, page 270 -- page 280 so we can have the remainder of the line. And this always refers to this person that would have been brought in at midnight on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I simply suggest to you, sir, that this person, that was brought in on the 15th at midnight, or at the time mentioned on this document is not one of the wounded prisoners that was transferred from Milici. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the names of the wounded Bosniaks from Milici, thus I can't say, looking at their names, whether it is them or it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me show you a document, and maybe that can help you, because I mean you were working at Zvornik Hospital so I'm sure you can help us with this document here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to have on e-court, please, P2451. I think we can go straight to, in the B/C/S version, is ERN number 8142, and we also have the English version. Now, this is a hospital discharge form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just out of an abundance of caution, if we could move into private session for this series of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem. Let's move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So, Witness, without referring to the person we were just talking about, that's one example, so you agree with me that there might be others. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: This one example indicates, yes, yes, that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now move to the two other persons that were referred to you by my colleague. And I'd like to go back to 1891, that's 61 ter 1891, on page 42 in English and page 333 in B/C/S. Now, my colleague has already asked this question. I will just ask you to confirm, again, because it is the introduction to my next question. My colleague representing another of the accused in this case asked you to confirm that the two individuals referred to - and I'm talking about on the left side of your screen, number 4904 and 4905 - and I guess they both have the name Alic, that both of these persons were those that you found on the exchange list in Bijeljina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, the fact, Witness, that these two persons are found in Bijeljina on the list and that they have been exchanged simply comforts you in your belief that all of these prisoners, after being taken to Standard - we're talking about the Milici prisoners - were indeed exchanged. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I just don't see the relevance of whether he's comforted or not by any particular information that he's being presented here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It's not for my colleague to answer this question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We think the witness should be given the opportunity to answer, but not exactly the way you put it. You need to rephrase it and perhaps you can ask him whether, having seen both documents now, including the one that was made use of by Mr. Sarapa, he wishes to state anything as to what he -- in relation to either of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer. One moment again.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. It may save some time ultimately in terms of whether I have any redirect or not. If my friend has any information to suggest that these 11 Milici prisoners are, in fact, on that exchange list that would we've seen today, then maybe we can short-circuit that and he can represent that or direct him to the document. Otherwise, I'll be forced to review each name and go through it. But if my colleague can direct us to the location on that document consistent with the question that he's asked, then that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, of course, I have no intention of doing that because the witness doesn't know any names. But now he knows four names that were used by my colleague, so I'm referring to these four names because we don't know the names of the other wounded prisoners. That's our difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead with your rephrased question, which I rephrased for you in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Doctor, my question is -- I will first do it in two parts to try to satisfy my colleague on the other side. According to the information that you were given at the time, it is your belief that these prisoners, after being taken from the hospital, were taken to Standard and were then exchanged. Is that your belief from the information you had at the time?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Before I answer your question, I must say that I am not familiar with any of the names. Looking at the logbook and the medical part filled in by the doctor, I can recall the wounds and the injuries, but I am not familiar with any of the names. I wasn't an eye-witness. I don't know when they arrived or when they left. What I do know was told to me at a meeting. At a morning meeting of the collegium, the chief said that the patients had been brought from Milici, that they are planned to be exchange, and until that happens they are going to be treated at our department. When they went to Standard, I specifically was entrusted with going to see them one day. Next time when I went to see them, they were not there, and a soldier they had been taken for exchange. This is what I know. I don't know anything else other than what the chief told me. And when I went to visit them the next time to examine them, they were not there and a soldier said that they had been taken for an exchange. That is all that I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, I perfectly understand that you are not familiar with the names of the people who were transferred, and that's just why I was focusing on these two that you have identified. By knowing what injuries they suffered and what injuries were treated, you identified two of those. And those are the ones that are before you at 490 -- 4904 and 4905, and those are the two people with the name Alic. And you saw that these two people are -- appear on the exchange list in -- of those who were sent to Bijeljina. So those two that you know and they were transferred, and that is in line with the information you received at the time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I objected to my statement, specifically in relation to those documents. It says I recall the names well, but that is not true, and I repeat that again. By looking at the logbook the part where I treated the patients, I recalled the patients and the type of injuries, and that I had treated the patients in the way that I described.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me take my question again and then we'll -- we'll leave it at that. The injuries that you did identify in the logbook, you will agree with me that these injuries go with the persons that we find at 4904 and 4905.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, he's been clear and consistent on direct and also on cross already, so I think this is wasting time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have pressure over here which I don't really need. I think we've heard enough on this, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Witness, I will ask you one last question concerning another individual which my colleague -- another name which my colleague raised with you. MR. BOURGON and that is on 1891, that's the 65 ter number, and page 275 in B/C/S, and page 21 in English. Can I have that on e-court, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Witness, I draw your attention to the serial number. You're looking at the left side of your screen, and that is 4582. And I would simply like to confirm with you, if we move to page 276, so we can have a complete picture of -- no, sorry. We have the information on this document. At 4582, you confirm that this patient was treated at 11.00. Is that correct, according to this information?

utterances.speaker: RADIVOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: That is written in this part of the logbook.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we'd like Dr. Novakovic to be done today. I will save the questions I referred to previously for another witness with respect to the prisoner list, so nothing further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. There are no further questions for you, Doctor, which means you are free to go. Our staff will assist you. On behalf of the Tribunal, I wish to thank you for having come over, and I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exhibits. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've --- THE FRENCH INTERPRETER: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- to two items now. The first being the witness statement, P02480, and the second being 65 ter 1884. The other two documents we used with the doctor have already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections? Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I am going to object to the admission of the witness statement. It seems to me that Rule 92 ter provides the Trial Chamber with a discretion to admit a witness statement in the case of a witness where three conditions are met. The first two, there is no problem. He is present in court, and he was available for cross-examination. But the third is that he attest the witness statement accurately reflects his declaration and what he would say if examined. And it seems to me in the case of this witness that's precisely what he did not do. And it would be very difficult to characterise such alterations as he made to his written statement as minor amendments. Just to pick one example, the witness statement which the Prosecution asked for you to receive into evidence says that the 11 wounded prisoners were not treated at the Zvornik Hospital. His account here today is quite the opposite to that. So my first submission is that the third condition under Rule 92 ter (A) is not met, and your discretion to admit the statement into evidence does not arise. The second point is, really, what is the purpose of it. This is a witness who has now been in evidence, I know there's been a bit of argument, but he's been in evidence for the best part of three hours plus. There is not one word of his account that you haven't heard that is relevant to these proceedings, and so the admission into evidence of his statement is oteos [phoen] redundant and simply surplus to requirements. Those are my objections in headline form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, but briefly, if my learned friend could direct us to precisely where in the witness statement it is alleged that he never said that these prisoners were treated at the Zvornik Hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we have to leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We can do it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The time is up, and I wouldn't like it take any of the other Chamber's court time. We stand adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00. We'll finalise this exercise and will proceed with the next witness, and I hope that by then you would have come to terms and agreement on the problems that were raised this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
